index.html.text:
FOR INDEPENDENT AUTO REPAIR SHOP OWNERS

Your door rate is not the rate you collect.

The number on the wall is $165. The number that reached the bank last month was $138.84, and nothing on any estimate said so. It went out as a coupon, a fleet account, a diagnostic hour thrown in to win the job, and a warranty claim paid at a rate somebody else set — none of which looked like a discount at the time. Put one month in below and see the real rate, exactly where the rest of it went, and what the posted rate would have to be to fix it.

What is my effective labor rate, and why is it lower than my door rate?

Should I keep taking warranty work?

The month you billed

One month, straight off your management system’s labor sales report. Hours are book hours billed, not clock hours.

Labor sales only — leave parts, sublet, shop supplies and fees out of these two dollar figures, or the rate comes out too high. Internal hours are the ones a technician turned and nobody was invoiced for: comebacks, policy adjustments, your own shop vehicles, and the courtesy check that found nothing.

The technicians

The same month, all technicians together. This is what turns a rate into a margin.

Clock hours are the hours you paid for, however your technicians are paid — hourly, flat rate, or a guarantee. Pay includes payroll taxes, workers’ comp and benefits, because those are the cost of the hour too. Service advisors and the parts counter are overhead below, not technicians here.

What the shop costs

The same month, from your profit-and-loss statement.

Overhead is everything that is not technician pay or the cost of parts: rent, utilities, advisors and office staff, insurance, software, marketing, and owner pay for the hours spent running the business. Parts gross profit is parts sales minus what the parts cost — it pays some of that overhead, and labor has to carry whatever is left.

What you actually collect

This is the worked example the form opens on — a three-technician shop, not yours yet. Change the figures and press the button.

Fill in a month and the rate appears here.

Questions shop owners ask

The same answers the page publishes as structured data, so a search result and a visitor read the same words.

What is an effective labor rate?

Labor dollars divided by the labor hours those dollars were billed against. If you sold 365 hours last month and collected $50,675 of labor, your effective labor rate was $138.84 — whatever the sign on the wall says. It is the only number that tells you what an hour of your shop's time is actually worth, and no report on an estimate performs the division.

Why is my effective labor rate so much lower than my posted rate?

Because the shortfall arrives in pieces that never look like a discount at the time. A coupon, a fleet or wholesale account, a diagnostic hour waived to win the job, book time trimmed to close a sale, and warranty claims paid at a rate somebody else sets. Each one is small and defensible on its own, and none of them shows up as a line called discount. This page adds them back up and splits the total between customer-pay work, which the shop controls, and warranty, which it does not.

Should comeback and internal hours be in the effective labor rate?

Not in the headline figure, and this page keeps them out of it. The industry measures the effective rate over hours that were sold, which is what your management system reports and what you can check in a minute. Comebacks, policy work and shop vehicles were never sold at all, so they are shown separately two ways: as an effective rate over every hour your technicians turned, and priced at your door rate as the revenue those bays could have produced. Their cost is already inside your cost per billed hour, because payroll paid for them.

Why does raising my door rate not fix the gap?

Because you collect a new rate in roughly the same proportion as you collected the old one. A shop realizing 84% of a $165 rate and needing $175 an hour to reach its target gross profit does not need a $175 door rate — it needs about $208, because the coupons, the fleet accounts and the warranty mix are still there. This page computes both numbers and shows them together. It is the single most common way a rate rise lands short of what it was meant to fix.

What is the difference between cost per clock hour and cost per billed hour?

Cost per clock hour is what you pay a technician for an hour they are at the shop. Cost per billed hour is that same payroll spread over only the hours you sold. If you pay for 480 hours and sell 365, a technician costing $40 a clock hour costs $52.60 inside every hour that reaches an invoice. The gap is technician efficiency, and it is why two shops with identical pay scales can have very different labor gross profit.

How do you decide how much overhead labor has to carry?

Parts gross profit pays what it pays, and labor carries the rest. The break-even labor rate here uses your monthly overhead minus your parts gross profit, floored at zero. That avoids inventing an allocation percentage between the parts and labor departments, which is always a guess, and both inputs are lines you can read straight off a profit-and-loss statement.

Is my shop's data uploaded anywhere?

No account and no network requests — the calculator runs entirely in your browser. There is deliberately no shareable link: what your shop bills, what it pays technicians, and what its fixed expenses are should not ride in a URL. Saving a scenario writes the figures to this browser's own storage so you are not retyping them next month; clearing your browser data clears them. The optional usage counter records only which features were used and the day, never a number from your month.

Is this an accounting opinion?

No. It is your own numbers, divided. It makes no determination about tax treatment, technician pay classification, warranty contract terms, or how any figure should be recorded, and it does not tell you what to charge or what work to accept — your market, your contracts and your judgement do that. Check every figure against your management system and your accounts, and against a qualified professional, before pricing work with it.

What this is, and what it is not

This page divides the numbers you typed. It has no way to know your market, your competition, your warranty contracts or your customers, so it does not tell you what to charge, what work to take, or what to pay anybody — it says what the month you entered actually did.

It is not an accounting, tax, legal or employment opinion, and it makes no determination about how any figure should be recorded or how any technician should be paid or classified. Check every number against your management system and your accounts, and against a qualified professional, before pricing work with it.

No warranty. This free tool is not legal, tax, accounting, insurance, employment or financial advice, and it does not tell you what to charge, what warranty work to accept, or how any technician should be paid or classified. It is arithmetic on the numbers you type. Verify every figure against your own management system, payroll records and accounts, and against a qualified professional, before relying on it or pricing work with it. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for loss or damage from its use.

Nothing leaves your browser. Every number stays on this device. Your labor sales, payroll, overhead and the rates worked out from them are never uploaded and never appear in a usage count — those are anonymous tallies of which features were used, stored locally. “Save this month on this device” writes the twelve figures to this site’s own browser storage so you are not retyping your month next time; clearing your browser data clears them. There is deliberately no shareable link: what a shop bills, pays and spends is more than should ever ride in a URL you might paste into a chat app.

Pricing a crew hour from the cost side instead, before any work is sold? The shop rate calculator works out the burden, overhead rate and hourly rate a trade job has to be sold at from payroll, vehicles and office costs — the forward-looking half of this question.

Selling tires and add-ons instead of repair orders? The tire shop ticket margin calculator turns each line’s price, parts, labor minutes and attach rate into net per ticket, and shows what a discount must win back.

Running a collision shop and weighing an insurer program? The collision shop DRP profit calculator puts your month with the program beside your month without it.

Running a detailing shop with more services than bay hours? The auto detailing service menu picker finds the set of services that earns the most inside your bay hours.

Running a maintenance or inspection contract rather than repair orders? The maintenance contract calculator prices recurring visits against the labor and parts they consume across a year.

Already running (or considering) a full shop management system? See this calculator vs. Tekmetric's shop dashboard, this calculator vs. Shop-Ware's shop dashboard, this calculator vs. Shopmonkey's shop dashboard, or this calculator vs. AutoLeap's labor rate calculator for how they differ.

Would rather just divide labor sales by hours off your own reports? You should — here is how to do it, and the four places that division gives a number you can’t act on.

Free and open source. If it changes what you charge, the code is under an MIT licence — support is entirely optional and never changes what the tool does.

should-i-keep-taking-warranty-work.html.text:
EFFECTIVE LABOR RATE CALCULATOR

Should I keep taking warranty work?

Warranty pays whatever the manufacturer sets — usually well below your door rate — so dropping it looks like an easy win for your effective labor rate. It is, on the rate. It is not automatically a win on profit, and the difference is entirely about what fills the hour you freed up.

Work out my own numbers →

The shop keeping warranty

Same three-technician shop as the rest of this calculator: $165 posted, 320 customer-pay hours at $145.00 an hour, 45 warranty hours at $95.00 an hour, 28 internal hours, $19,200 of technician pay, $34,000 of overhead and $21,000 of parts gross profit.

FigureThis month
Effective labor rate$138.84
Labor sales$50,675
Labor gross profit$31,475 (62.1%)
Profit before tax$18,475

Warranty is $3,150 of this month's $9,550 billing gap — 33%. Refusing it looks, on that line alone, like the obvious fix.

Two ways to stop taking it — and they end differently

Refuse the 45 warranty hours and one of two things happens to that time. Either nothing replaces it, or customer-pay work does. Both raise the effective labor rate to the same number. Only one of them raises profit.

OutcomeEffective rateLabor salesProfit before tax
Keep the warranty work$138.84$50,675$18,475
Drop it, bay sits empty$145.00$46,400$14,200
Drop it, backfilled with customer-pay work$145.00$52,925$20,725

Both alternatives post the same $145.00 effective rate, because the $95 warranty hours are what were pulling the blended number down — whether or not anything replaces them changes nothing about the average of what is left. But one alternative costs the shop $4,275 a month against keeping the work, and the other gains $2,250. A rate improving from $138.84 to $145.00 reads as good news either way. Only the profit line says which one actually happened.

The question the rate can't answer

An empty bay produces nothing. Technician pay and overhead do not fall because a technician has no warranty ticket in front of them, so every dollar of warranty labor sales that isn't replaced by something else comes straight off the bottom line — $4,275 this month, about $51,300 a year at this mix. The rate goes up because the denominator (hours sold) fell along with the numerator (labor dollars), and a $95 hour disappearing from both sides of that ratio moves the average even when nothing good happened.

So the real question is not "does warranty pay less than my door rate" — it always does. It is: if I turn this hour away, what takes its place? A shop with a waitlist, a scheduler booked past the warranty repair's own turnaround window, or customer-pay jobs it is already declining for lack of a bay has an answer: a $145 hour. A shop with open capacity has no answer, and the hour just goes empty.

How to tell which shop you are

  1. Check your scheduler for the weeks around when warranty work typically lands. If customer-pay appointments are being pushed out past your own acceptable wait, you have replacement demand.
  2. Run the calculator with your own warranty hours zeroed out and internal hours raised by the same amount — that is the empty-bay case.
  3. Run it again with those hours added to customer-pay hours and sales at your own customer-pay rate instead — that is the backfilled case.
  4. Compare profit before tax, not the effective rate, between the two. The rate will look identical either way.

Nothing here says whether to accept a specific warranty claim, a specific manufacturer's reimbursement schedule, or how any repair order should be coded — only what the arithmetic does to a month's numbers under each assumption.

Work out my own numbers →

Common questions

Should I keep taking warranty work?

It depends on what fills the bay if you don't. On a shop billing $95 an hour on warranty against a $165 posted rate, dropping it and leaving the bay empty cuts monthly profit before tax from $18,475 to $14,200 — a real loss, even though the effective labor rate looks better at $145.00. The same drop with the hours backfilled by customer-pay work instead raises profit to $20,725. Same new rate, opposite outcome, because the rate alone does not say what happened to the hour.

Why does dropping warranty work raise my effective labor rate?

Because the effective labor rate is a blend, and warranty is usually the lowest-paying hour in it. On the worked example, warranty reimburses $95 an hour against a $165 posted rate, while customer-pay work already collects $145. Removing the $95 hours from the average — whether or not anything replaces them — pulls the blended rate up to the customer-pay rate of $145.00. The rate moving is arithmetic, not evidence that the shop is better off.

Does a higher effective labor rate always mean more profit?

No. The effective labor rate is dollars per hour sold — it says nothing about how many hours were sold. A shop that drops 45 warranty hours and leaves the bay empty sells fewer hours at a higher average rate, and on the worked example that costs $4,275 a month in profit even though the rate improved. A rate and a profit total can move in opposite directions whenever the hours behind them change.

How much profit do I lose if I drop warranty work and the bay sits empty?

On the worked example, exactly the warranty labor sales that disappeared: $4,275 for the month, or roughly $51,300 a year at the same mix. Technician pay and overhead do not fall just because the bay is empty, so every dollar of warranty labor sales that isn't replaced comes straight off the bottom line.

When does it make sense to stop taking warranty work?

When the shop already has more customer-pay demand than bay capacity — a waitlist, hours turned away, or a scheduler that is full past the warranty work's own turnaround window. In that case the warranty hour is not idle time being given up, it is customer-pay time being displaced, and swapping it for a $145 hour instead of a $95 one is a straightforward gain. A shop with open bays has no customer-pay work waiting to take the warranty hour's place, so refusing it just empties the bay.

Related

Want the full breakdown of where this month's gap came from, not just the warranty slice? See what is my effective labor rate. Pricing the hour from the cost side instead, before any work is sold? The shop rate calculator builds a required hourly rate up from payroll, vehicles and office costs.

No warranty. This page and the calculator it describes are not legal, tax, accounting, insurance, employment or financial advice, and they do not tell you what to charge, what warranty work to accept, or how any technician should be paid or classified. The worked example is an illustration, not a benchmark for your market or your manufacturer's reimbursement schedule. Verify every figure against your own management system, payroll records and accounts, and against a qualified professional, before relying on it or deciding what work to accept. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for loss or damage from its use.

vs-autoleap.html.text:
← Effective Labor Rate Calculator

This calculator vs. AutoLeap's labor rate calculator

AutoLeap, a cloud-based shop management platform for independent auto repair shops, publishes its own free labor rate calculator as a lead-generation tool. Based on AutoLeap's own description of it, that calculator asks for three numbers — your effective labor rate (labor dollars collected last month, divided by labor hours sold), your highest-paid technician's hourly rate, and your shop's technician productivity percentage — and turns them into a recommended rate to charge and an affordable technician wage. It shows the result after you submit your name, email, phone number and business name.

That makes it a tool for a different step than this page: AutoLeap's calculator assumes you already know your effective labor rate and helps you decide what to charge from there; this page computes the effective labor rate itself, from twelve figures a shop already has on a P&L or a management-system report, with no contact form and no account, and splits the gap between your posted door rate and your collected rate into three pieces with different fixes: customer-pay discounting, warranty shortfall, and comeback or internal hours priced as forgone capacity.

AutoLeap also sells a paid shop management platform — repair orders, digital vehicle inspections, parts ordering, technician time clocks, scheduling and customer communication all run through it — and its own reporting separately surfaces an effective labor rate figure once a shop's activity lives inside the platform, the same category of comparison as a full shop management system generally.

QuestionWhere to answer it
I already know my effective labor rate and want a recommended rate to charge and an affordable tech wage, and I don't mind submitting my contact details to see it. AutoLeap's free calculator — that is exactly what it is built for.
I don't yet know my effective labor rate — I have labor sales, hours, discounts, warranty and payroll figures, and I want the rate computed from those, with the gap explained. This calculator — type twelve figures you already have, get the rate and a three-way breakdown of the gap, with no contact form.
I want repair orders, DVIs, parts ordering, scheduling and technician time clocks running through one system, with the effective labor rate reported as part of that. AutoLeap's paid platform — that is what a shop management system is for, and the figure is one of many reports it produces once your operations live inside it.
I want this number with no account, no contact form, and nothing installed. This calculator — every figure is computed in your browser from what you type, and nothing is uploaded anywhere.

The two are not competing for the same first step. A shop that already knows its effective labor rate and wants a recommended charge-out rate gets that from AutoLeap's free tool, in exchange for a contact form. A shop that wants the rate computed from numbers it already has, split into the three causes that have different fixes, with nothing submitted anywhere, gets it here.

This calculator needs no account, no contact form and no integration: it is a static page, and every number is computed in your browser from what you type. Nothing about your labor sales, payroll or overhead is uploaded anywhere.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or AutoLeap's labor rate calculator?

They start from different places. AutoLeap's free tool asks you to type in your effective labor rate as an input — alongside your top technician's hourly pay and your shop's productivity percentage — and it computes the posted rate you would need to charge, showing the result only after you submit your name, email, phone number and business name. This page computes the effective labor rate itself, from twelve figures most shops already have on a P&L or a management-system report, with no contact form and no account, and it also works out the posted rate a target gross profit would really require.

Does AutoLeap's tool split the gap the way this page does?

No. Based on AutoLeap's own published description of the tool, it takes your effective labor rate as a given and turns it into an affordable technician wage and a recommended rate to charge — it does not break the gap between your door rate and your collected rate into discounting, warranty shortfall, and comeback or internal hours the way this page does. AutoLeap's paid shop management platform separately reports an effective labor rate figure as part of its own dashboard, once a shop's repair orders run through it; that is a different comparison from the free calculator, covered above.

Is this page affiliated with AutoLeap?

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by AutoLeap. AutoLeap is a trademark of its owner, named here only to describe what this calculator is and is not, based on AutoLeap's own public description of its tools and software.

Open the Effective Labor Rate Calculator to work out your own shop's number and the posted rate your target gross profit would really require.

No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It is not tax, legal, accounting, employment or financial advice, and it does not replace a qualified professional. Verify every figure against your own management system and accounts before relying on it or pricing work with it.

Best-effort hosting, no SLA. This tool is free and experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. We do not promise uptime, backups of anything you type, or that a URL will keep working.

Free and open source. If it changed what you charge, GitHub Sponsors is optional and never changes what the tool does.

vs-dividing-labor-sales-by-hours.html.text:
← Effective labor rate calculator

This calculator vs. dividing labor sales by hours yourself

Names no specific product or company. This compares a free calculator against the generic method every shop owner already has: pulling labor sales and labor hours off your management system's own reports and dividing one by the other.

First — the division is right, and you should do it

Labor sales ÷ the labor hours they were billed against. That is the effective labor rate, it is one line of arithmetic, and your DMS already prints both numbers on reports you run anyway. If you take nothing else from this page, take that: it is the single most useful figure most shops are not looking at, and no tool is required to get it.

What follows is not an argument that the division is hard. It is the four places the division gives a number you cannot act on, and each of them is a place a hand calculation quietly picks an answer without telling you it chose.

The worked example

Every figure below comes from this calculator's own starting numbers — a three-technician shop with a $165 posted rate, one month: 320 customer-pay hours billing $46,400, 45 warranty hours billing $4,275, 28 internal and comeback hours billed to nobody, and 480 technician clock hours paid.

QuestionDividing it yourselfThis calculator
The headline rate $50,675 ÷ 365 = $138.84 — correct, and the same number this page reports $138.84, plus the realization ratio it implies: you collect 84 cents of every posted dollar
Which hours you divided by Whichever column the report happened to show. Sold hours give $138.84; the 393 hours actually consumed give $128.94 — a $9.89 difference from the same sales figure Reports both, labelled: an effective rate on hours sold and an effective rate on all hours consumed
Customer-pay vs. warranty Blended into one number unless you deliberately pull and divide the two separately Split out: $145.00 customer-pay, $95.00 warranty — and the shortfall apportioned 67% / 33% between them
Unbilled hours Invisible. Nobody was invoiced for the 28 comeback and internal hours, so they appear in no labor-sales figure and change no division Priced at the posted rate — $4,620 this month, about $55,440 a year — and carried into cost per billed hour
What an hour actually costs Usually payroll ÷ clock hours: $19,200 ÷ 480 = $40.00 $40.00 a clock hour, but $52.60 inside every hour you bill, because you sold 365 of the 480 hours you paid for (76% efficiency)
The rate a target gross profit needs Commonly set to the required rate itself — which then gets collected at the same 84% and lands short $175.34 must reach the invoice for 70% labor gross profit, so the posted rate has to be $208.39
History across months Its real strength — a row per month, per tech, or per advisor, tied to your own export Prices one period at a time and saves no history; it does not replace a tracking sheet
Where the numbers go Your file, your machine Also your machine — the arithmetic runs in your browser and nothing you type is uploaded

The four places the division goes quiet

1. It does not say which hours it used

Sold hours and consumed hours are different, and on these figures they are 28 hours apart. The same $50,675 of labor sales is either $138.84 an hour or $128.94 an hour depending on which denominator the report you grabbed happened to contain. Both are real numbers; only one answers "what did I collect for an hour I sold". A hand calculation makes that choice silently.

2. A blended rate averages two problems with different fixes

$138.84 is the average of $145.00 of customer-pay work and $95.00 of warranty work. Customer-pay discounting — coupons, fleet rates, waived diagnostic time, book hours trimmed at the counter — is money the shop gave away and can stop giving away. Warranty shortfall is a rate somebody else sets, and the only lever is how much of that work you take. Reading one blended number tends to send a shop at whichever of those is loudest rather than whichever is biggest. Here it is customer-pay, at 67% of a $9,550 monthly gap.

3. Unbilled hours cannot appear in a sales figure

The 28 hours that went to comebacks, policy work and shop vehicles produced no invoice, so they are in no labor-sales total and no division will ever surface them. Payroll paid for them regardless, which is why they show up instead as the difference between $40.00 a clock hour and $52.60 a billed hour. At the posted rate those bays represented $4,620 of capacity this month.

4. A target rate is not the rate you post

This is the one that costs real money. If 70% labor gross profit needs $175.34 to land on the invoice, posting $175.34 does not deliver it — you would collect roughly 84% of it, about $147.54, for the same reason you collect 84% of $165 today. The posted rate that actually realizes $175.34 is $208.39. Every rate rise that "didn't work" is a candidate for this arithmetic.

When your spreadsheet is the better tool

For tracking, it plainly is. This page has no memory: close it and the month is gone. A sheet with a row per month — or per technician, or per service advisor — tied to your own DMS export is how you see a trend, and that is a thing this calculator does not do and is not trying to do. The sensible arrangement is both: work one month out here to see where the gap sits and what the required posted rate is, then log the result in your own file.

Every figure on this page is the calculator's own worked example, not a claim about any real shop and not an industry benchmark. Your mix, your rates and your reports will produce different numbers — the point is which numbers to produce, not what they should come out to.

Common questions

Can I just divide labor sales by labor hours myself?

Yes, and you should — it is one line of arithmetic and your management system already prints both numbers. Pull labor sales and the labor hours they were billed against for the same period and divide. That single figure is the most useful number most shops are not looking at. The reasons this page exists are what the division does not tell you: which hours you divided by, that a blended rate hides two very different rates, that unbilled hours never appear in it at all, and that the posted rate a target gross profit requires is not the rate the target names.

Which hours should I divide by — sold hours or clock hours?

For an effective labor rate, divide by the hours you actually billed against, not the hours you paid for. Those are different numbers and they give different answers. On this page's worked figures, dividing $50,675 of labor sales by the 365 hours sold gives $138.84; dividing the same sales by the 393 hours consumed — the sold hours plus 28 internal and comeback hours nobody was invoiced for — gives $128.94. Neither is wrong, but they answer different questions, and a hand calculation rarely says which one it did. The calculator reports both and labels them.

Why does a blended effective rate hide the problem?

Because customer-pay and warranty work are paid at rates you control to very different degrees. On the worked figures the blended rate is $138.84, but customer-pay collected $145.00 an hour and warranty collected $95.00. Those have different fixes: customer-pay discounting is a pricing and counter-process problem, warranty shortfall is a mix problem whose only lever is how much of that work you accept. A shop reading only the blended number tends to attack whichever cause is most visible rather than the largest. On these figures customer-pay is 67% of the shortfall and warranty is 33%.

If I need a 70% labor gross profit, why can I not just post that rate?

Because you will collect the new posted rate in roughly the same proportion you collect the current one. On the worked figures a 70% labor gross profit needs $175.34 to actually reach the invoice — but at the 84% realization the shop is currently running, posting $175.34 collects about $147.54. The posted rate that delivers $175.34 of realized rate is $208.39. This gross-up is the step a spreadsheet almost always misses, and it is why a rate rise worked out by hand usually lands short of what it was meant to fix.

Does this calculator replace my spreadsheet?

No, and for tracking it should not. This page prices one period at a time and saves no history, while a spreadsheet's real strength is a row per month, per technician or per service advisor, tied to your own DMS export. Many shops would use both: this calculator to get one month's arithmetic right and see where the gap sits, and their own sheet to log the result and watch the trend over a year.

Open the effective labor rate calculator →

No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It is not tax, accounting, insurance, employment, legal or financial advice, and it does not replace a qualified professional. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it, and for meeting any obligation it helps you prepare for. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

vs-shop-ware.html.text:
← Effective Labor Rate Calculator

This calculator vs. Shop-Ware's shop dashboard

Shop-Ware, a cloud-based shop management system for independent auto repair shops, is where a subscribing shop runs its repair orders, digital vehicle inspections, parts ordering, technician time clocks, scheduling and customer communication. Its reporting includes a dashboard figure for effective labor rate, computed automatically from the shop's own activity once that activity lives inside the platform.

That makes it a different tool for a different moment than this page: an ongoing operating system a shop pays for and runs its whole workflow through, versus a single free calculator for the one question “what did an hour of labor actually collect last month, and where did the rest of it go.” This page does not manage repair orders, parts, scheduling or technician clock-ins, and it never will — it takes twelve figures you already know, from any management system or a spreadsheet, and divides them.

QuestionWhere to answer it
I want repair orders, DVIs, parts ordering, scheduling and technician time clocks running through one system, with the effective labor rate reported as part of that. Shop-Ware — that is what a shop management system is for, and the figure is one of many reports it produces once your operations live inside it.
I want this month's effective labor rate right now, from numbers I can already read off my current system or P&L, with no account and no migration. This calculator — type twelve figures, get the rate and the breakdown in under a minute.
I want the gap between my door rate and my collected rate split into discounting, warranty and unbilled hours, with each priced separately. This calculator — that split, and the posted rate a target gross profit would really require after realization, is what this page exists to compute.
I want the number to update itself automatically every month as repair orders close, with no retyping. Shop-Ware or a comparable shop management system — this page has no connection to your point-of-sale and reads nothing automatically; you save a month's figures to this browser instead.

The two are not competing for the same job. A shop already running (or ready to run) its whole operation through a management system gets the number as a byproduct of that system's reporting. A shop that is not — or one that wants the breakdown this month, on the numbers it already has, before deciding whether a new system is worth the switch — gets it here for free, with no account and nothing installed.

This calculator needs no account and no integration: it is a static page, and every number is computed in your browser from what you type. Nothing about your labor sales, payroll or overhead is uploaded anywhere.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or Shop-Ware's dashboard?

They answer the question at two different costs. Shop-Ware is a paid, subscription cloud shop management system: repair orders, digital vehicle inspections, parts ordering, technician time clocks, scheduling and customer communication all run through it, and its reporting computes an effective labor rate automatically once a shop's whole workflow lives inside the platform. This page computes the same underlying number — labor dollars collected over labor hours billed — from twelve figures you type once, taken from whatever management system or spreadsheet you already use, with no account, no migration and no monthly cost. It is not a shop management system and does not touch repair orders, parts, or scheduling.

Shop-Ware's public description of its dashboard reports effective labor rate as one figure among the metrics it surfaces; this page was built to answer nothing else. what-is-my-effective-labor-rate.html.text:
EFFECTIVE LABOR RATE CALCULATOR

What is my effective labor rate?

It is your labor sales divided by the labor hours you billed them against — and for most independent shops it is 15 to 30 per cent below the rate on the wall. The gap is not a decision anyone made. It is the sum of a lot of small ones, and the only operation that reveals it is a division your management system never performs.

Work out my effective labor rate →

The arithmetic, on one real month

Take a three-technician shop with $165 on the wall. Last month it billed 320 customer-pay hours and collected $46,400 of customer-pay labor. It billed 45 warranty hours and was reimbursed $4,275. Its technicians also turned 28 hours on comebacks, policy work and the shop’s own truck, which nobody was invoiced for.

Labor only. Parts, sublet, shop supplies and fees are excluded from both dollar columns.
WorkHours billedLabor collectedPer hour
Customer pay320.0$46,400$145.00
Warranty45.0$4,275$95.00
Sold365.0$50,675$138.84
Internal and comebacks28.0$0—
Every hour turned393.0$50,675$128.94

The effective labor rate is $138.84: $50,675 over the 365 hours that were sold. Against $165 posted, that is $26.16 an hour gone, or $9,550 across the month — about $114,600 a year at the same mix.

Where the $9,550 went

It splits cleanly into two causes with nothing in common except direction, which is why the total on its own is not enough to act on:

CauseThis monthWhat it is, and who controls it
Customer-pay discounting$6,400320 hours that could have billed $52,800 at the posted rate and billed $46,400. Coupons, fleet and wholesale rates, waived diagnostic time, book hours trimmed to close. Every dollar of it was given away by the shop.
Warranty rate shortfall$3,15045 hours reimbursed at $95 against $165 posted. The rate is set by whoever pays the claim, so the only lever is how much of this work the shop takes on — a decision about mix, not about pricing.

The 28 internal hours are deliberately not in that total. They were never sold, so there is no billing gap to attribute — but the bay, the lift and the technician were consumed, and at the posted rate that is $4,620 of capacity the month did not earn. Their payroll cost is already counted somewhere else, which is the next section.

Why a $40 technician costs $52.60 an hour

The shop paid for 480 technician clock hours and sold 365 of them — 76% efficiency. Payroll, including burden, was $19,200. That is $40.00 per clock hour, and $52.60 per hour that actually reached an invoice, because the 115 unsold hours have to be recovered inside the 365 that were sold.

This is the figure that makes two shops with identical pay scales and identical posted rates end the year very differently. It is also why efficiency and effective rate have to be read together: a shop can lift its rate and lose the gain to a drop in efficiency without either number looking wrong on its own.

Why raising the door rate recovers less than you expect

The shop above collects 84 cents of every posted dollar. Suppose it wants 70% labor gross profit. At $52.60 of cost per billed hour, that needs an effective rate of $175.34.

The mistake is to post $175.34. The coupons, the fleet agreements and the warranty mix do not go away when the sign changes, so a $175.34 door rate collects about 84% of it — roughly $147, and the target is missed again. To collect $175.34 at 84% realization, the posted rate has to be about $208.39.

That is the whole argument for measuring realization rather than only the rate: it is the multiplier on every pricing decision a shop makes, and it is the reason rate rises so often disappoint the person who authorised them. The alternative to a bigger rise is to move realization itself — fewer standing discounts, less waived diagnostic time, or less warranty work — and the split above says which of those is worth the effort at this shop.

How to get the numbers out of your own month

  1. Run your management system’s labor sales report for one complete month. Take labor dollars only — if parts, sublet, shop supplies or fees are in the figure, the rate comes out too high.
  2. Split it into customer pay and warranty, with the book hours billed against each.
  3. Find the hours your technicians turned on internal, comeback and policy work. These are often on repair orders with a zero total.
  4. Take technician clock hours and technician payroll including taxes, workers’ comp and benefits, from payroll. Service advisors and the parts counter are overhead, not technicians.
  5. Take total overhead and parts gross profit from the month’s profit-and-loss statement.

That is twelve numbers, all from reports you already run. The calculator does the rest in your browser — nothing is uploaded, and there is deliberately no shareable link for a page that holds a month of your shop’s finances.

Work out my effective labor rate →

Common questions

What is my effective labor rate?

Your labor sales for a period divided by the labor hours those sales were billed against. Take last month's labor sales — customer pay plus warranty, with parts, sublet and shop supplies excluded — and divide by the book hours you billed. A shop that sold 365 hours and collected $50,675 of labor has an effective labor rate of $138.84, whatever the posted rate says.

Why is my effective labor rate lower than my posted rate?

Because the difference leaves in pieces that never look like a discount. Coupons and specials, fleet and wholesale accounts on a standing discount, a diagnostic hour waived to win the job, book time trimmed at the counter to close a sale, and warranty work reimbursed at a rate set by whoever pays the claim. Each is defensible on its own and none appears as a line item called discount, so the only way to see the total is to divide labor sales by labor hours.

What is a good effective labor rate?

There is no universal figure, because it depends on your market, your mix and your posted rate. The useful comparison is against your own numbers rather than someone else's: what share of your posted rate you actually collect (realization), and whether the rate covers technician cost plus the overhead your parts gross profit does not. A shop realizing 84% of its door rate has a different problem from one realizing 96%, even if both collect the same dollars.

Should comebacks be included in the effective labor rate?

Not in the headline number. The standard measure uses hours that were sold, which is what your management system reports and what you can check against it. Comebacks, policy work and shop vehicles were never sold, so they belong beside the figure rather than inside it — as an effective rate over every hour turned, and priced at your door rate as the capacity those bays did not earn. Their payroll cost is already inside your cost per billed hour.

Will raising my door rate fix my effective labor rate?

Only in proportion to what you already collect. If you realize 84% of your posted rate, a $10 rise reaches the invoice as about $8.40, because the coupons, fleet agreements and warranty mix that took the first 16% are still in place. A shop needing a $175 effective rate at 84% realization needs a posted rate near $208, not $175. This is the most common reason a rate rise lands short of what it was meant to fix.

What is technician efficiency and how does it change my labor gross profit?

Efficiency is the hours you billed divided by the clock hours you paid for. Below 100%, payroll for hours that produced nothing billable has to be recovered inside the hours that did. A technician costing $40 a clock hour at 76% efficiency costs $52.60 inside every hour that reaches an invoice, which is why two shops with the same pay scale and the same posted rate can have very different labor gross profit.

Related
